questions.q: Does PostgreSQL have a built-in audit subsystem comparable to Oracle's Unified Auditing, per this lesson?
options: Yes — PostgreSQL's Unified Auditing feature works identically to Oracle's
No — PostgreSQL has no way to log any SQL activity at all
No — PostgreSQL's own logging settings aren't designed as a compliance-grade audit trail, and pgAudit is the real, standard answer
Yes — log_statement = 'all' is specifically designed and marketed as an audit trail
questions.explain: PostgreSQL lacks a built-in, dedicated audit subsystem; ordinary logging settings are general-purpose, and pgAudit is the widely adopted extension that fills this gap.

questions.q: What is pgAudit, per this lesson?
options: A PostgreSQL extension providing structured, audit-grade logging, widely supported by major cloud providers
A GUI tool unrelated to logging or auditing
A replacement for pg_hba.conf
A built-in core feature of every PostgreSQL installation with no setup required
questions.explain: pgAudit is described as an extension — not a core feature — but one so widely adopted (including by AWS RDS, Azure, and Google Cloud SQL) that it functions as the de facto standard.

questions.q: Which of these is a real pgaudit.log statement class mentioned in this lesson?
options: backup, covering pg_dump and pg_basebackup operations
vacuum, covering autovacuum activity
ddl, covering CREATE, ALTER, and DROP statements
replica, covering streaming replication traffic
questions.explain: The lesson lists read, write, ddl, role, and misc as real pgaudit.log statement classes; ddl covers CREATE/ALTER/DROP.

questions.q: How does this lesson honestly compare pgAudit to Oracle's Unified Auditing?
options: pgAudit is a core PostgreSQL feature that predates Oracle's auditing capability
pgAudit and Oracle's Unified Auditing are architecturally identical in every respect
Oracle has no auditing capability at all, unlike PostgreSQL
Oracle's auditing is a dedicated core subsystem with its own structured audit trail, while pgAudit is a trusted extension writing into PostgreSQL's general log stream
questions.explain: The lesson draws an honest architectural distinction: Oracle's auditing is a first-class core subsystem, while pgAudit writes structured entries into PostgreSQL's own log stream rather than a separate dedicated audit store.

questions.q: Why is ordinary log_statement = 'all' logging insufficient for compliance purposes, per this lesson?
options: It cannot be enabled in postgresql.conf under any circumstances
It is verbose and unstructured, built as a debugging and monitoring tool rather than a compliance-grade audit trail
It logs absolutely nothing about SQL activity
It only works when pgAudit is also installed
questions.explain: The lesson explains that general-purpose logging like log_statement wasn't designed with structured, filterable audit requirements in mind, unlike pgAudit.
